questions.question: List the five statements of the Kinetic Molecular Theory and explain how diffusion and Brownian motion serve as evidence for the model.
questions.expected_answer: One: all matter is made of particles — atoms, molecules or ions. Two: the particles are in constant, random motion. Three: the particles possess kinetic energy, and their average kinetic energy increases as temperature rises. Four: there are spaces between the particles. Five: forces of attraction — intermolecular forces — act between the particles, and their strength relative to the particles' kinetic energy decides the state. Diffusion is one substance spreading through another purely by the random motion of its particles — the smell of a peeled orange crossing a still room, or a drop of food colouring tinting a whole glass of unstirred water — and it runs faster in gases and at higher temperatures, matching statement three. Brownian motion is sharper evidence: pollen grains in water or smoke specks in air jerk along jagged paths under a microscope; being far too large to move themselves, they must be bombarded unevenly from all sides by invisible, permanently moving particles — direct support for statement two.

questions.question: For each of the three states, describe the particle arrangement, motion and forces, and show how the energy-versus-forces contest explains the bulk properties.
questions.expected_answer: Solid: particles closely packed in a fixed, regular lattice, vibrating about fixed positions; the forces are strong and the kinetic energy too small to overcome them — hence fixed shape, fixed volume, near-incompressibility and high density. Liquid: particles still close together in an irregular arrangement, sliding past one another; the forces remain significant but the particles have enough kinetic energy to leave fixed positions while staying held in the body of the liquid — hence fixed volume, no fixed shape, and still hard to compress. Gas: particles far apart in rapid, random, straight-line motion, colliding with each other and the walls; the forces are negligible against the particles' large kinetic energy — hence no fixed shape or volume, easy compression because most of the volume is empty space, low density, and pressure that is nothing but wall collisions. The one pattern: forces winning gives a solid, a rough match gives a liquid, kinetic energy winning gives a gas; heating adds kinetic energy and cooling removes it, so every change of state is the contest tipping.

questions.question: Describe the heating curve of half a kilogram of ice from minus fifteen degrees to steam, and explain in terms of energy why the temperature stops rising at the plateaus and why the boiling plateau is longer.
questions.expected_answer: The curve has five parts: a rising line from minus fifteen to zero as the ice's particles gain kinetic energy and vibrate faster; a horizontal plateau at zero where ice and liquid water coexist while melting; a rising line from zero to one hundred as all-liquid water warms; a much longer plateau at one hundred where liquid and steam coexist while boiling; and a rising line above one hundred as pure steam heats further. The temperature stops rising at the plateaus because temperature measures average kinetic energy, and during a change of state the supplied energy is spent overcoming the forces of attraction between particles — raising their potential energy and prising them into a freer arrangement — rather than speeding them up; energy is still being added continuously, doing a different job. The boiling plateau is markedly longer because separating liquid particles completely from one another into a gas takes far more energy than merely loosening a lattice into a liquid. The cooling curve mirrors this exactly, the plateaus now releasing energy as the forces re-form — which is why condensing steam burns so badly — and state reads off the curve by position: solid below zero, solid plus liquid on the first plateau, liquid between, liquid plus gas on the second, gas above.
